source.title_on_document: The effects of generative AI usage on employee innovation: Collaboration modes, idea journey, and decline in creative psychological ownership

supplement.where: Appendix A. Supplementary data: 'Supplementary data to this article can be found online at https://doi.org/10.1016/j.technovation.2026.103700' (p. 25)
supplement.holds: From the in-text references: A.1 Study 1 scenarios, A.2 Study 2 scenario, A.3 the DeepSeek task interface, A.4 the Study 4 collaboration-mode manipulation, A.5 the LLM used (DeepSeek-V3.2 thinking mode); Supplement B measure details; C.1-C.6 Tables S1-S6 (competing mediators and alternative control specifications); D.1-D.11 Tables S7-S32 (serial, stage-specific, and nonlinear analyses); E.1-E.9 with Tables S33-S35 (contextual and network factors). No creativity ratings or diversity measures of outputs are mentioned. This inventory is based on the main article's references (pp. 6-22); the separate supplement is not included in the saved PDF and was not independently inspected. The references identify no output-creativity or output-diversity statistics.

paper_design_summary: Studies 1 and 2 randomly assigned imagined GAI-use or collaborator scenarios without actual AI assistance, whereas working adults in Studies 3 and 4 generated marketing ideas with an embedded DeepSeek interface under high or low usage requirements. Study 4 additionally randomized collaboration mode during marketing-copy refinement and analyzed 305 people; Study 5 surveyed employees in China in two waves. The focal measures concern self-reported creative psychological ownership and intentions to elaborate, champion, and implement ideas; no creativity or diversity score on the ideas or copy is reported.

eligibility.reason: Criterion 1 is met by Study 4: participants were randomly assigned to six conditions varying actual DeepSeek usage and collaboration mode on a marketing-copy task (pp. 14-15, Section 7.2). Criterion 2 is met by its 305 people analyzed (p. 16, Tables 7-8, n = 305); this is not a separately reported count at random assignment. Criterion 3 is not met: the focal measures are self-reported creative psychological ownership and innovation-related intentions, with no reported creativity or diversity score on participants' outputs (p. 6, Section 4.2; p. 7, Section 5.2; p. 11, Section 6.2; p. 15, Section 7.3; p. 19, Section 8.2). The limitations explicitly state that creative psychological ownership was assessed primarily through self-report (p. 24, Section 11). Study 3 does not explicitly state random assignment in its methods, but this does not alter the paper-level criterion 1 finding from Study 4. Studies 1-2 involve imagined assistance, and Study 5 measures workplace GAI use observationally. The separate supplement is not in the saved PDF; its in-text descriptions identify task materials, measures, and additional analyses of the reported constructs, without identifying output creativity or diversity scores. Exclude from the core and context datasets: the randomized AI study reports self-reported outcomes rather than a qualifying scored output.

one_line_finding: Higher assigned GAI usage lowered self-reported creative psychological ownership in Study 4 (high vs low M = 3.93 vs 4.12, reported Cohen's d = .30; p. 15, Section 7.4.3), with an internal meta-analytic GAIU-CPO estimate of −.184 across the five studies (p. 22, Table 14), but no output-creativity or output-diversity scores are reported.
open_questions: Study 3 never states that assignment to high vs low usage was random (p. 10 says only 'one-factor between-subjects experimental design'); the introduction calls the experiments randomized in general (p. 2).
Arm-level counts are not given for Studies 1, 3, and 4; Study 2 reports randomized arm counts but does not separately state analyzed arm counts.
Studies 2 and 4 name no recruitment platform or country; their population is coded from the paper's description of employed or working adults.

Study 3 collected ideas and Study 4 produced refined copy (pp. 11, 14-15), but no creativity or diversity scores on those outputs are reported; the separate supplement has only been described through the article's in-text references.
notes: Each study lists its focal self-reported CPO measure with scored_on_output = false to document the outcome exclusion; the self-reported intention outcomes (IE, IC, II) are summarized in measure_detail. No qualifying output-based outcome is reported in the main article or identified by its supplement references; the separate supplement was not inspected. The internal mini meta-analysis (p. 22, Section 9 and Table 14) pools these five studies: GAIU→CPO −.265, −.238, −.181, −.147, −.188; meta-analytic −.184; CPO→IE .383, IC .401, II .403. It is not a synthesis or reanalysis of another paper's experiments. The final review covered the entire markdown conversion, including Appendix A and the references, and checked the recorded numerical results and participant counts against extracted PDF text. Spec alignment: Study 2 is coded other because its randomized vignette experiment has no stated recruitment or administration setting; Study 3 is coded other because its between-subjects manipulation does not explicitly establish random assignment (pp. 7, 10-11). These codes do not assert nonrandom assignment. Study 2 analyzed arm counts are left null because only assigned arm counts and the overall analyzed count are separately printed. Unstated countries remain not_stated; analyzed counts, measurement locators, and the limits of the supplement inventory are explicit. The reconciliation object is retained unchanged as the earlier review history. No c119 challenge files were present; final resolution counts refer only to challenge problems. In final.open_items, affects_eligibility refers to whether the unresolved detail can change the paper-level criteria, not merely a descriptive field of an already nonqualifying study.

open_items.item: Study 3 does not explicitly state random assignment (pp. 10-11, Sections 6.1.1-6.1.3). Authors could confirm the allocation method; this would clarify Study 3 but cannot change the paper-level random-assignment criterion already met by Study 4 (p. 14, Section 7.2), or supply a qualifying outcome.

Arm-level counts for Studies 1, 3, and 4 and separately stated analyzed arm counts for Study 2 are unavailable in the article. Authors could supply allocation and exclusion counts; this does not affect the sample-size criterion because study-level analyzed totals are confirmed, including 305 for Study 4 (p. 16, Tables 7-8).

Studies 2 and 4 do not state recruitment platform or country, and Study 2 does not state the administration setting (p. 7, Section 5.1.1; p. 14, Section 7.1). Authors could clarify these descriptive fields; they do not determine any core eligibility criterion.

The existence of ideas and refined copy in Studies 3-4 does not establish a scored-output outcome. The article reports ownership and intention scales (p. 11, Section 6.2; p. 15, Section 7.3), identifies no creativity or diversity scoring of these artifacts, and describes the reliance on self-report (p. 24, Section 11). No further information is needed to exclude the reported outcomes; obtaining raw unscored text alone would not change criterion 3.
